position_in_era.historical_role: A structural inversion of the Hetfield/Hammett dual-protagonist formula: Hetfield wrote the song privately for himself, and plays the guitar solo himself — Hammett does not appear on the studio recording. The dialectic collapses into a monologue: the same person who sings also solos. This inversion reveals the structural assumption of all the other dual-protagonist songs: that the voice and the guitar solo ARE different characters, played by different people.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded at One on One Studios and Eldorado Studios, Los Angeles (1990–1991). Producer: Bob Rock, who suggested adding an orchestral component. Michael Kamen orchestrated the string arrangement. Hetfield played the guitar solo himself — one of the few Metallica songs where he solos. Hammett is absent from the studio recording entirely. Duration: 6:29.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Hetfield as sole protagonist: he wrote the song privately while on tour ('bumming out about being away from home'), did not initially intend to release it, and only shared it with the band during pre-production. The decision to have Hetfield play the solo himself (rather than handing it to Hammett) was Hetfield's own. The solo is understated — not a showpiece — which may reflect that it was not meant to be a rival protagonist but an extension of the vocal's own voice.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Hetfield: acoustic guitar, electric guitar, lead guitar solo. Hammett: absent (studio recording). Ulrich: drums. Newsted: bass. Michael Kamen: orchestral arrangement. Bob Rock: producer (also contributed piano on Black Album).
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: The Black Album, Metallica's mainstream breakthrough. 'Nothing Else Matters' became one of the most-covered Metallica songs and is frequently paired with Guns N' Roses' 'November Rain' as a defining 1991 power ballad — two songs from the same year whose structural DNA is related but divergent.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Album August 1991; single April 1992. The song was the third single from the album. The orchestral arrangement by Kamen positions the vocal in an operatic context — but with no separate guitar protagonist, the aria has no soloist to answer it.
